item.title: Federal Accessibility: Agencies Not Consistently Meeting the Information and Communication Technology Needs of People with Disabilities
item.description:
What GAO Found
Section 508 of the Rehabilitation Act of 1973 generally requires federal agencies to develop, procure, maintain, and use information and communication technology (ICT) that is accessible to people with disabilities. ICT includes things such as websites and electronic forms. According to governmentwide guidance, agencies should test ICT for accessibility before it is deployed. However, in 2025, most federal agencies responding to a federal survey reported inconsistent testing. Further, GAO found that three selected agencies—Department of Homeland Security (DHS), Department of Agriculture (USDA), and Department of Housing and Urban Development (HUD)—varied in the extent to which they followed leading practices from the General Services Administration (GSA) and Office of Management and Budget (OMB) for pre-deployment testing.
DHS generally follows leading practices, and it was taking action for continuous improvement to address testing gaps for certain types of ICT.
Both USDA and HUD partially follow leading practices. For example:
USDA has a Section 508 policy, but the policy is outdated, and there is no accompanying manual, thereby leading to gaps in clear guidance for testing. HUD has a policy, but due to staffing resources, paused some implementation efforts that affect testing, such as filling key positions, updating procurement forms, and verifying testing results.
When ICT is not tested, agencies cannot ensure federal services and information are accessible to members of the public and federal employees with disabilities.
According to disability groups and researchers GAO interviewed, federal agencies’ formal complaint processes were sometimes lengthier and more complex than informal agency feedback processes. While submitting feedback can be easier for individuals, GAO’s covert testing found that agencies did not consistently fix identified issues. Fourteen of the 23 agencies to which GAO covertly provided feedback fixed the issues that GAO identified from September 2025 through February 2026. Nine agencies had not fixed the issues identified as of May 2026. (See figure.)
Agency Responses to Feedback on Information and Communication Accessibility Issues Submitted Through GAO’s Undercover Investigation
Note: For more details, see fig. 2 in GAO-27-107934. GAO notified these agencies regarding the investigation results and related General Services Administration guidance.
Why GAO Did This Study
Federal agencies provide services through ICT such as websites, electronic documents, and kiosks. If ICT is not accessible, millions of Americans who have a disability may be unable to access these services. Section 508 generally requires federal ICT to be accessible, but GSA and others have reported that federal ICT accessibility has been a persistent challenge.
This report (1) describes what federal agencies report about testing ICT for accessibility and assesses the extent to which selected agencies followed related leading practices and (2) describes factors that may affect people’s use of formal complaint processes compared with feedback processes and assesses the effectiveness of agencies’ feedback processes. 
GAO reviewed documents and interviewed officials at three agencies—DHS, HUD, and USDA—selected for variation in size, their public-facing services, and other factors. GAO compared agency actions to leading practices from GSA and OMB guidance. GAO also reviewed 23 agencies’ formal complaint and feedback processes and websites. After identifying accessibility issues for each agency, GAO covertly submitted feedback to monitor agencies’ responses. GAO also interviewed officials from GSA and the U.S. Access Board and researchers and representatives from disability groups.
